newsitem.title: USA: Herman tells Lott of role in White House meetings.
newsitem.headline: Herman tells Lott of role in White House meetings.

text.p: Cabinet nominee Alexis Herman met Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott Friday to explain her role in controversial White House coffee meetings that has stalled her confirmation as labour secretary.

Lott told reporters after the 30-minute talk in his office that Herman had told him she did not invite Currency Comptroller Eugene Ludwig to a White House meeting of bankers that had been arranged by the Democratic National Committee.
The meeting is at the centre of a controversy over the perception of linkage between campaign fund-raising and access of business leaders to the White House.
President Clinton admitted on Tuesday that Ludwig should not have been included in the gathering that mixed bankers and a federal regulator who exercises authority over them.

Lott said Herman told him that some of the press accounts about her activities as director of the White House public liaison office had not been accurate and that she had agreed to his suggestion that she provide clarifying documents to the Senate Labour Committee.
"She says she was not at the meeting with the regulators and she did not invite Mr. Ludwig to be there," Lott told reporters.
But Lott said Herman told him her office was involved in arranging the meeting and mistakes were made in handling it.
"She says some of the things attributed to her (in the press) were not accurate," Lott said.
Herman, who did not speak to reporters during her visit to the Capitol, is one of two presidential nominees who have run into trouble in the Senate.

Former National Security Adviser Anthony Lake, nominated as CIA director, is under fire for his admitted failure to notify Congress that the administration was turning a blind eye to the flow of Iranian arms to Bosnian Moslems in 1994 despite a U.N. arms embargo.

Also, the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section is investigating Lake's failure to comply immediately with a ruling by the White House legal counsel that he needed to sell some energy stocks in order to avoid a potential conflict of interest. White House officials said it was an oversight.
Presidential spokesman Mike McCurry said earlier Friday the White House was confident the two will eventually be confirmed.
Lott, a Mississippi Republican, has publicly said he believes Herman might have come close to violating the Hatch Act, which bars federal officials from partisan activities.

He said Friday the meeting helped answer some of his questions. But he said the problems over the nomination could remain "unless some further clarification can be provided, and she said she could do that."

Thus far, the Senate has confirmed four of Clinton's nominees with little dissent -- Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Andrew Cuomo and Commerce Secretary William Daley.
